title: ISC U2·W2 — The Trust Services Criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality & Privacy (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — what a SOC 2 actually measures

A SOC 2 report is only as meaningful as the criteria it tests against. Those are the Trust Services Criteria (TSC) — five categories that define what it means for a system to be trustworthy: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy. This week works through each, the relationships among them, and the distinction the exam loves to test — confidentiality versus privacy. These criteria are the substance of the ISC discipline's security domain and the yardstick by which any service organization's controls are judged.

Security — the common criteria

Security is the foundational category, also called the common criteria, and it is required in every SOC 2 engagement. It addresses protection of the system against unauthorized access — both logical and physical — covering the access controls, boundary protections (firewalls, encryption), change management, and monitoring from ISC Unit 1. Because the other four categories all depend on a secure system, Security underlies them: there is no meaningful availability, integrity, confidentiality, or privacy without it. A SOC 2 that includes only Security still says something important; one that omits it is impossible.

Availability

Availability addresses whether the system is available for operation and use as committed or agreed — the uptime and performance a service-level agreement promises. It is not about functionality or usability; it is about access. The relevant controls include capacity and performance monitoring, environmental protections, backup and recovery, and the business continuity and disaster recovery plans (covered in Week 4) that keep the system reachable through disruptions. A cloud customer that depends on a provider being up chooses a SOC 2 that includes the Availability category.

Processing Integrity

Processing Integrity addresses whether system processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized — in short, whether the system does what it is supposed to do, correctly. It maps directly to the application controls from ISC Unit 1 (input, processing, and output controls): data is validated on entry, processed without error, and produced completely and on time. Importantly, processing integrity concerns the processing, not the underlying data's correctness if bad data was supplied — "garbage in" is the user's problem, but the system must not corrupt good data. It is the criterion a payment processor or a calculation engine must meet.

Confidentiality

Confidentiality addresses whether information designated as confidential is protected as committed — encompassing trade secrets, business plans, intellectual property, and any sensitive business information a contract or policy marks confidential. Controls include encryption, restricted access, and proper retention and disposal. Confidentiality applies to any sensitive information, regardless of whether it concerns people — a merger plan or a proprietary algorithm is confidential business data. This breadth is exactly what distinguishes it from the next, narrower category.

Privacy — and how it differs from confidentiality

Privacy addresses the collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal of personal information in conformity with the entity's privacy notice and established privacy principles. The key exam distinction: privacy applies specifically to personal information about individuals (names, Social Security numbers, health and financial data), while confidentiality applies to any sensitive information, personal or not. Privacy is also broader in scope of obligation — it covers the full life cycle of personal data and an individual's rights (notice, choice, access), reflecting privacy regulations. A trade secret is confidential; a customer's medical record is both confidential and a privacy matter.

How the criteria combine in an engagement

A service organization chooses which TSC categories its SOC 2 covers, based on what it commits to customers — Security is mandatory, and the others are added as relevant (a hosting provider adds Availability; a health-data processor adds Confidentiality and Privacy). Within each category, the controls are evaluated against points of focus that illustrate what meeting the criterion looks like. The result is a tailored report: two SOC 2s can cover different category sets, so a user must check which criteria a given report actually addresses before relying on it for a particular concern.

The criteria as a control framework

Beyond SOC reporting, the Trust Services Criteria function as a practical framework for designing and assessing controls over any system. They translate the abstract goals of ISC Unit 1 — govern, secure, control — into testable objectives an organization can build toward and an auditor can examine. Mastering the five categories, the mandatory role of Security, and the confidentiality-versus-privacy line gives a candidate the vocabulary the ISC discipline is built on and the lens through which modern systems assurance is performed.

The common criteria and points of focus

The five categories share a backbone: the common criteria (the Security category) are organized like COSO's components — control environment, communication and information, risk assessment, monitoring, and control activities — adapted to information systems. Each criterion is accompanied by points of focus: illustrative attributes that help the organization and the auditor judge whether the criterion is met (for example, points of focus under Security describe boundary protection, identity management, and threat detection). The points of focus are not a checklist to satisfy line by line; they are guidance for exercising judgment about whether the underlying objective is achieved.

Mapping controls to the criteria

In practice, a service organization maps its actual controls to each selected criterion to demonstrate coverage — a single control (multi-factor authentication, say) may support several criteria (Security and, by protecting access to personal data, Privacy). Gaps in the mapping reveal criteria with no supporting control, which the organization must remediate before the examination. This mapping discipline mirrors the skill graph applied to learning: relate each concrete control to the objective it serves, so that coverage — and gaps — become visible. An auditor likewise traces from each criterion to the control and the evidence that it is met, so an unsupported criterion cannot hide.

CMA bridge

When MBG selects a cloud vendor for sensitive payroll and employee data, the relevant SOC 2 should cover Security (always), Availability (the system must be up), Confidentiality (protect the business data), and Privacy (protect employees' personal information). Knowing which criteria matter for which data lets the CFO ask the vendor for the right report.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the five TSC: Security (mandatory common criteria), Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy.
  2. Security underlies all others (protection from unauthorized access); Availability = system available as committed (uptime/DR); Processing Integrity = complete/valid/accurate/timely/authorized processing.
  3. Distinguish Confidentiality (ANY sensitive information) from Privacy (PERSONAL information about individuals, full life cycle + rights, per the privacy notice).
  4. A service org chooses which categories its SOC 2 covers (Security required); check which criteria a report addresses before relying on it.

Recap: the Trust Services Criteria define a trustworthy system across five categories — Security (the mandatory common criteria protecting against unauthorized access and underlying all others), Availability (the system is up as committed), Processing Integrity (processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized), Confidentiality (any designated sensitive information is protected), and Privacy (personal information is handled across its life cycle per the privacy notice); the exam line is that confidentiality covers any sensitive data while privacy is specifically about individuals' personal information; and a SOC 2 covers whichever categories the service organization selects, with Security always required.

flashcards.back: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy. Security is the mandatory 'common criteria'; the rest are added as relevant.
Protection of the system against unauthorized (logical + physical) access. Required in every SOC 2; underlies all the other categories.
The system is available for operation and use as committed/agreed (uptime, SLA). About access, NOT functionality. Controls: capacity monitoring, backup/recovery, BCP/DR.
System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized — the system processes correctly. Maps to input/processing/output application controls. (Doesn't fix bad input data.)
Information DESIGNATED confidential (trade secrets, IP, business plans — any sensitive info, personal or not) is protected via encryption, access limits, proper disposal.
Personal information about individuals is collected/used/retained/disclosed/disposed per the entity's privacy notice + principles, including individual rights. Specific to people.
Confidentiality = ANY sensitive information. Privacy = specifically PERSONAL information about individuals (full life cycle + rights/regulations).
The service organization selects which categories its SOC 2 covers (Security always required); a user must check WHICH criteria a report addresses before relying on it.

questions.q: Which Trust Services category is required in every SOC 2 engagement?
questions.explain: Security (the common criteria) is mandatory and underlies the other categories.

questions.q: The Availability criterion concerns whether the system is:
choices: Available for operation and use as committed
questions.explain: Availability is about access/uptime as committed — not functionality or usability.

questions.q: Processing Integrity means system processing is:
choices: Complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized
questions.explain: Processing Integrity addresses correct, complete, authorized processing — mapping to application controls.

questions.q: The key difference between Confidentiality and Privacy is that Privacy applies to:
questions.explain: Privacy is specific to individuals' personal information; confidentiality covers any sensitive information.

questions.q: A trade secret or a proprietary algorithm is protected under which criterion?
questions.explain: Sensitive business information (not about individuals) falls under Confidentiality.

questions.q: Who selects which Trust Services categories a SOC 2 will cover?
choices: The service organization (with Security always required)
questions.explain: The service organization chooses the categories based on its commitments; Security is mandatory.

questions.q: Privacy controls address personal information across its:
choices: Collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal
questions.explain: Privacy covers the full life cycle of personal information per the privacy notice and principles.
